extracted.intended_audience: policy analysts, regulators, researchers, journalists, and general public interested in rulemaking public comments (e.g., FCC/net neutrality)
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and assessing quality, authenticity, and provenance of public comments submitted to administrative rulemaking dockets (illustrated with the 2017 FCC net neutrality comment record). Focuses on detecting duplicates, organized campaigns, and fraudulent/impersonated submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the 21.7 million comments posted, only 6% were unique; the other 94% were submitted multiple times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the proportion of unique comment texts versus duplicates to assess how much of the docket reflects distinct individual input rather than repeated templates. High duplication rates indicate lower substantive variety and potential organized campaigns. Example: in this case only 6% uniqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identical or near-identical text across many submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Identical or near-identical text across many submissions is evidence of low-quality or orchestrated comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag comments that are verbatim or nearly the same as many others; these suggest use of form letters or script-driven submissions rather than individualized engagement. Use string similarity detection, clustering, or exact-match counts to identify these clusters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of submissions around a few top templates
rubrics_metrics.description: The seven most-submitted comments (six of which argued against net neutrality regulations) comprise 38% of all the submissions over the four-month comment period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculate how much of the docket is dominated by a small number of message templates or top-submitted comments. High concentration (large share from a few templates) suggests coordinated campaigns and reduces docket diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traceability/coordination to specific organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: The text of many of the top comments can be traced back to a small number of organizations (e.g., battleforthenet.com; Taxpayers Protection Alliance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether common text originates from organizational websites, advocacy groups, or campaign landing pages. Tracing wording back to a few sources indicates coordinated outreach rather than independent individual submissions. Document examples and counts (e.g., combined text from three suggested comments appeared in ~2.4 million submissions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraudulent or impersonated comments (astroturfing)
rubrics_metrics.description: More than 8.5 million fake comments that impersonated real people were submitted to the FCC; disguising an orchestrated, paid campaign as a grassroots effort is often referred to as astroturfing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect impersonation (fake names, stolen identities, or fabricated profiles) and quantify suspected fraudulent submissions. Look for patterns consistent with paid lead-generation or deliberate identity misuse. Example: lead generators like Fluent, Inc. (~4.8 million fraudulent comments), Opt-Intelligence, Inc. (>250,000), and React2Media, Inc. (~329,000) were implicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission patterns inconsistent with stated identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Submission patterns inconsistent with stated identities (timing, geography) can indicate non-genuine comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze metadata such as timestamps, submitter location claims, and frequency patterns. Rapid bursts of submissions, identical timing across many entries, or geographic distributions that contradict claimed residence are red flags for inauthentic or automated campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Email addresses tied to lead-generation services
rubrics_metrics.description: Email addresses tied to lead-generation services are an indicator of orchestrated campaigns rather than individual submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check submitter contact information for domains or address patterns associated with lead generators or mass-signup services. Presence of such addresses supports classification of comments as generated through recruitment/paid channels rather than organic individual engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive, unique engagement with the proposed rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of unique substantive engagement with the proposed rule is a marker of low-quality comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a comment addresses the specific provisions, reasoning, evidence, or consequences of the proposed rule versus offering generic or off-topic statements. High-quality comments typically provide original arguments, specific references to the rule text, data or personal experience relevant to the rule, and tailored recommendations.
